title: How Horizon became £1.8B+ redress — and counting
narrative_md:
**It took a four-part ITV drama to finish a job Parliament, the courts and three prime ministers had failed to do for two decades.**

On 1 January 2024, ITV aired 'Mr Bates vs The Post Office.' Within a week, 1.3 million people had signed a petition demanding justice. Within five months Parliament had passed emergency legislation quashing hundreds of convictions. The Horizon scandal is now the most expensive miscarriage of justice in British history — £1.8 billion in redress and rising.

Between 1999 and 2015 the Post Office prosecuted more than 700 sub-postmasters for theft, fraud and false accounting, using data from the Fujitsu-built Horizon IT system as evidence. The software had bugs — the Post Office knew it had bugs, as the Clarke Advice of 2013 made painfully clear — yet prosecutions continued and exonerations were resisted. Lives were destroyed: four suicides are directly linked to the scandal; dozens of sub-postmasters died before seeing their names cleared.

The Horizon Convictions Redress Act 2024, passed in May and given Royal Assent on 24 May 2024, did what the Court of Appeal had been unable to: quash convictions en masse, by statute, without requiring individual case review. It was constitutionally extraordinary — Parliament acting as a court of appeal — and politically unavoidable after the ITV drama turned a specialist injustice into a national cause.

Financial exposure to the Department for Business and Trade, which sponsors Post Office Ltd, has ballooned. The Horizon Shortfall Scheme, GLO scheme, Overturned Convictions scheme and Horizon Convictions Redress Scheme together have paid out over £600 million, with total commitments exceeding £1.8 billion. Treasury officials privately expect the final bill to exceed £2.5 billion once legal costs, interest and Fujitsu's share are resolved.

Sir Wyn Williams's statutory inquiry delivered its final report on 8 July 2025, identifying systemic failures at senior Post Office and Fujitsu levels and recommending criminal referrals. The Metropolitan Police's Operation Olympos is investigating potential perjury and perverting-the-course-of-justice offences against up to 45 individuals.

The money flow is now a Treasury problem. Because DBT compensation is funded from the Consolidated Fund, rising redress costs feed directly into borrowing and, in the long chain, into debt interest. The scandal that was triggered by a buggy accounting system has become a structural fiscal commitment.

The drama's real power was that it reframed sub-postmasters as protagonists. For 20 years they were defendants. In 90 minutes of Sunday-night television, they became heroes — and the state found it could no longer afford to disagree.
